issues.legal_issue: A legislature may retrospectively alter the legal basis of an earlier judgment and thereby render that judgment ineffective when it acts within its legislative competence, complies with the Constitution, and removes the defect or basis on which the judgment rested.
material_facts: An earlier judgment directed that the value of coal stock on the eve of nationalisation be taken into account in settling the mine owner's claim.

A later amendment retrospectively declared that the scheduled compensation had always included the value of coal stock and enacted a provision validating payments and accounts notwithstanding contrary court judgments.
The amendment changed the legal basis on which the earlier judgment had directed that the stock value be included.
issues.conclusion: The retrospective amendment was effective to alter the legal basis of the earlier judgment and render its direction ineffective; this did not amount to an impermissible exercise of judicial power.
issues.legal_principle: Legislatures have plenary power to legislate prospectively and retrospectively within their assigned fields, subject to legislative competence and constitutional limits. A validating law can neutralise a judicial decision only by removing the defect or changing the legal basis on which that decision rested; merely declaring that a judgment is not binding is insufficient. The Court applied Shri P.C. Mills Ltd. v. Broach Borough Municipality and relied also on West Ramnad Electric Distribution Co. Ltd. v. State of Madras, Udai Ram Sharma v. Union of India, Tirath Ram Rajindra Nath v. State of U.P., Krishna Chandra Gangopadhyaya v. Union of India, Hindustan Gum & Chemicals Ltd. v. State of Haryana, and Utkal Contractors and Joinery (P) Ltd. v. State of Orissa. It distinguished D. Cawasji & Co. v. State of Mysore because the amendment there had not removed the defect. The relevant provisions were the retrospective amendment to Section 10 of the Coking Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1972 and the validating provision in Section 19 of the 1986 Amendment Act.

rule.if: validating_legislation_challenged and prior_judgment_exists and retrospective_legislation_enacted and legislative_competence and constitutional_compliance and legal_basis_changed

predicates.validating_legislation_challenged: A party brought a proceeding challenging legislation that was intended to affect the legal effect of an earlier judgment.
predicates.prior_judgment_exists: A court had previously decided the relevant legal issue and issued a direction based on the law then in force.
predicates.retrospective_legislation_enacted: The legislature enacted a law that applies from a time before its enactment.
predicates.legislative_competence: The legislature acted within the subject matter on which it had power to legislate.
predicates.constitutional_compliance: The retrospective law did not violate a constitutional restriction.
predicates.legal_basis_changed: The later law altered or removed the legal basis on which the earlier judgment rested.

issues.definition: When a challenged retrospective law is enacted by a competent legislature, complies with constitutional limits, and changes the basis of an existing judgment, that judgment no longer controls the matter.

issues.legal_issue: Where retrospective law deems compensation to include the value of coal stock existing immediately before nationalisation, that stock value is not separately payable or included in accounts for the earlier period of government management.
material_facts: The mine remained owned by its private owner while its management was held by the government custodian before nationalisation.
Coal raised during the management period remained in stock immediately before the mine vested in the government.
An earlier court direction required the stock value to be credited when accounts for the management period were recast.

The retrospective amendment deemed the scheduled compensation to include the value of the stock, and the validating provision barred proceedings seeking further payment on the ground that the stock value had not been included.
issues.conclusion: No further compensation was payable for the stock, and its value was not to be taken into account in the management-period accounts.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 10(2), as retrospectively introduced into the Coking Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1972, scheduled compensation was deemed always to include the amount payable for coal stock and specified assets existing immediately before the appointed day. Section 19 of the 1986 Amendment Act validated the relevant payments and accounts and barred proceedings seeking further sums on that ground. Applying those provisions, the Court held that neither a separate payment for the stock nor inclusion of its price in the management-period accounts was required. It distinguished the earlier decision in Central Coal Fields Ltd. v. Bhubaneswar Singh because the retrospective amendment had changed the legal basis governing the stock.

rule.if: interim_management_accounting_dispute and ownership_retained_during_management and pre_transfer_stock_exists and retrospective_compensation_includes_stock

predicates.interim_management_accounting_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether stock value must be included in accounts for a period when the government managed a mine before nationalisation.
predicates.ownership_retained_during_management: The owner retained title to the mine while the government or its custodian managed it.
predicates.pre_transfer_stock_exists: Coal raised from the mine remained in stock immediately before the transfer of ownership to the government.
predicates.retrospective_compensation_includes_stoc: A retrospective law treats the compensation payable for the mine as already including the value of the pre-transfer stock.

issues.definition: If a dispute concerns interim management accounts, the owner retained title during government management, pre-transfer stock remained, and the compensation is retrospectively treated as including that stock, the stock is excluded from those accounts and no separate payment is due.
